procedural_history.impugned_order: Acquittal of all three accused by the Sessions Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Bhimappa) applied to the Mysore High Court under Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for special leave to appeal against the acquittal of the three respondents. The High Court dismissed the petition on November 28, 1966, stating that the petitioner had no locus standi to prefer an appeal when the State had prosecuted the respondents in the Sessions Court. A revision application filed by the appellant was also rejected.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment and order of the Mysore High Court. The Supreme Court held that the appellant was entitled to a hearing of his petition for special leave under Section 417(3) and remitted the case to the High Court for this purpose.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant, a private complainant whose case was tried alongside a police-instituted case, was entitled to file a petition for special leave to appeal against an acquittal under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: Following an incident, the police filed a charge-sheet against two accused individuals.
The appellant, dissatisfied that a third person was not charged, filed a separate private complaint against that third person.
The two cases were tried together, but they maintained separate identities and case numbers, and separate acquittal orders were recorded for each.
The Sessions Court acquitted all three accused.

The appellant applied to the High Court for special leave to appeal the acquittals under s. 417(3), but the High Court dismissed the petition, ruling that the appellant had no 'locus standi' (right to bring the action) because the State had prosecuted the case.
law: Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure grants a complainant the right to apply for special leave to appeal an acquittal, but only if the acquittal was passed in a "case instituted upon complaint."
The Supreme Court identified this requirement—that the case must be one instituted upon a complaint—as the essential condition for a private complainant to have the right to appeal.
application: The Court analyzed whether the appellant's case met the condition of being "instituted upon complaint."
It found that there were clearly two distinct cases: one instituted by the police and the other instituted by the appellant's private complaint.

The Court rejected any notion that the private complaint case had merged with the police case. It reasoned that the identity of the two cases was maintained throughout the trial, evidenced by the fact that they proceeded under their own case numbers and resulted in separate acquittal orders.
Because the appellant's case was instituted upon his complaint and remained a distinct legal case until the end, the requirement of s. 417(3) was fulfilled.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was entitled to file a petition for special leave to appeal under s. 417(3) because his case was instituted upon his complaint and never lost its separate identity. The Court overturned the High Court's decision and remitted the case back to the High Court to hear the appellant's petition.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prior rejection of the appellant's revision application could extinguish his statutory right to move the High Court for special leave to appeal against the acquittal.

facts: The appellant had previously filed a revision application, which was rejected.
He also applied for special leave to appeal against the order rejecting his revision, and that was also refused.
It was argued that these prior rejections should conclude the matter and prevent him from seeking special leave to appeal the acquittal.
law: The right to move the High Court for special leave to appeal against an acquittal under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a statutory right.
application: The Supreme Court explicitly disagreed with the argument that the failed revision application should end the matter.
The Court reasoned that the appellant's statutory right to move the High Court for special leave could not be lost or extinguished by the fact that a revision application had been filed and rejected.
It held that the outcome of the revision had "no bearing" on the separate matter of the statutory right to seek special leave to appeal the acquittal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court concluded that the prior rejection of the appellant's revision application did not extinguish his statutory right to move the High Court for special leave to appeal against the acquittal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant, a private complainant whose case was tried alongside a police-instituted case, was entitled to file a petition for special leave to appeal against an acquittal under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's case was instituted on a private complaint, distinct from the case instituted on the police report.
There was no merger of the two cases, as their separate identities were maintained throughout the trial, with the appellant's case proceeding on its own number.
Although evidence was led together, the acquittal was recorded separately in each case.
Therefore, the appellant's case remained a 'case instituted upon complaint' under s. 417(3), entitling him to move the High Court for special leave to appeal.
respondent_arguments: The appellant (petitioner) had no locus standi to prefer an appeal.
The right to appeal is lost because the State had prosecuted the respondents in the Sessions Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellant's statutory right to move the High Court is not lost or concluded by the fact that a separate application for revision was rejected, and the result of the revision has no bearing upon the matter.
obiter: In criminal jurisdiction, the word 'case' ordinarily means a proceeding for the prosecution of a person alleged to have committed an offence, which results in either a discharge, conviction, or acquittal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A private complainant's case, instituted upon a complaint, does not lose its distinct identity simply because it is tried alongside a case instituted on a police report. Where the two cases maintain their separate identities throughout the trial, evidenced by separate case numbers and separate acquittal orders, the complainant's case remains a "case instituted upon complaint." Consequently, the complainant retains the statutory right under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to move the High Court for special leave to appeal the acquittal, and this right is not extinguished by the prior, unsuccessful pursuit of a separate revision application.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if a case is "instituted upon complaint" for the purposes of s. 417(3) when tried jointly with a police case, the court examines whether the identity of the two cases was maintained throughout the trial. Factors include whether the complainant's case proceeded on its own number and whether the acquittal was recorded separately for each case.

The court applied the principle that a distinct statutory right, such as the right to seek special leave to appeal, cannot be extinguished by the pursuit of a different legal remedy, such as a revision application, as the outcome of the revision has no bearing on the existence of the separate statutory right to appeal.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning protects a party's statutory rights from being inadvertently lost due to procedural conveniences, such as holding a joint trial for a police case and a private complaint case.

The decision upholds the principle that different legal remedies (like revision and appeal) are distinct and the failure of one does not automatically preclude the pursuit of another, unless statutorily specified.
